- **`main` does not take the I/O park either, while the pool is carrying tasks.** It waits on the runtime's bell, and everything that could wake it rings that — a completion the pilot noticed, a `Slot` filled by a task, a task finishing. Without it a `.join()` across a thread would be a `main` asleep in the kernel that no pool thread could reach, which on the completion path is a hang rather than a delay.
- **Four states per task, and the fourth is the whole reason for the other three.** A future is out of its cell while it is being polled, so a waker arriving then must not queue it — and if it only declined, the wake would be lost and the task would sit idle for ever. It is recorded instead, and the worker that finishes the poll re-queues. A test wakes a future from inside its own poll to hold that.
- **One Nikaia line, two lowerings**: `TaskHandle::start_on_pool` at `yes` and `TaskHandle::start` at `no`. Two functions and not one with a bound, because the bound belongs to the *build*: a program at the default is never asked for a `Send` its setting does not need, which is what keeps [ADR-061](docs/specification/adr/adr-061.md) D1's plain count reachable from inside a task. ADR-006 D5's drain asks both queues, so *"a task nobody joins still runs"* is as true on the pool as on the thread.
- **What is not built is D6's `Send` as a refusal of ours.** The pool's starter asks for it, so a task holding something that may not cross is refused — by `rustc`, about the generated file, which Part III C.1 calls a bug in this compiler. [#254](https://github.com/Nikaia-Language/Nikaia/issues/254) carries it with what it needs: ADR-005 §1 Group B's structural check already runs on what a task *captures*, and what it has never been asked about is what a body holds **across a pause**.

### Fixed (a build switch changed in the manifest rebuilds the program)

- **It did not, and nothing said so.** A build switch is not a source, so nothing Cargo watches changes when one does — and the lowering happens inside the `rustc` wrapper, which Cargo runs only for a package it already thinks is stale. Flipping `user-parallelism` in `nikaia.toml` therefore left the package fresh and the program running at the setting it was **built** at. The cache had the switch as a dimension ([ADR-021](docs/specification/adr/adr-021.md) D5) and nothing ever got as far as asking it.
- **The third member of a family this build already knew.** A generated file rewritten with identical bytes is newer than Cargo's fingerprint, so the package is dirty for ever; the dependency file `rustc` emits names the generated Rust, so an edited `.nika` left the package fresh. Both were fixed by giving Cargo the right file. So is this one: the driver writes the resolved switches to `target/nikaia/gen/switches` before `cargo` runs — only when they differ, so an unchanged switch dirties nothing — and the wrapper puts that file into the dependency file beside the `.nika` sources. A switch that changed is an input that changed.
- **The driver and not the wrapper writes it**, which is the whole of why it works: the wrapper only runs for a package Cargo has already decided to rebuild, so a file written there could never be what caused the rebuild.
- Found while measuring the `yes` executor, which is the shape of it: the switch decided nothing visible until it decided which executor a task ran on. The test flips it **four** times, because the first flip passed before the fix — Cargo had something else to rebuild — and only going back caught it.

### Removed ([ADR-050](docs/specification/adr/adr-050.md) D1 and D7: statements run in the order they are written)

- **The automatic overlapping is withdrawn, and the measurement is the reason.** [ADR-033](docs/specification/adr/adr-033.md) grouped adjacent statements whose touch sets met on nothing and ran them together; it was adopted **provisional and unmeasured**, and building it produced the measurement — **127 adjacent pairs across `examples/`, zero of which overlapped**. What a reader was asked to hold was a rule about statement order that no program in this repository ever used, and that is a bad trade at any price. `overlap { … }` is what replaces it, and D1's own argument is that a programmer saying where an overlap may happen is worth more than a compiler guessing.
- **`seq { … }` and the `ordering` switch go with it** (D7), because both exist only to turn the inference off. `seq` has left the reserved words — 30 down to 29, so a program may call a variable `seq` again — and `ordering` is no longer a manifest key, a CLI flag, or a [ADR-021](docs/specification/adr/adr-021.md) D5 build-cache dimension. A switch that selects between two behaviours when there is only one left is a question with no answer.
- **What survives is the touch sets, in the stronger use of them.** `touches` is still a ledger column, the resource kinds are still the vocabulary, and `verdict` still answers why two operations may not run together — but it now **checks a claim the program made** instead of making one of its own, which is `NK2104`. ADR-033 D9's refusals outlived the feature they were written for, word for word, and `--overlaps` still prints them: about the blocks a *program* wrote rather than about every adjacent pair.
- **The vehicles the inference chose are gone from `std` too**, since nothing can reach them: `task::both` (the pool's closure pair), `task::interleave` (its twin for halves that pause, now `task::overlap2`) and `task::read_pair` (D10's free pair of reads). `fs::read_both` stays — it is the pair a *program* asks for, and it always overlaps because somebody wrote it. `benches/overlap --bin runtime` calls `rayon::join` directly so ADR-033 §8.4's number, the ~46 µs a closure pair costs, stays reproducible after the vehicle that used it went: that number is why D2's vehicle takes futures.
- **A manifest that still writes `ordering` now fails**, which it did not: the key stayed on the accepted list after the setting behind it went, so a build read it, ignored it and said nothing — a program differing from the file that describes it. It is refused in its own words rather than as a misspelling, because whoever wrote it meant it, and the refusal names `overlap { … }`. The distinction is why there are two lists: a **moved** key (`cleanup-deadline`) still decides something elsewhere, so the manifest keeps working and says where to look; a **withdrawn** one decides nothing anywhere.
- Also gone with it: the compiler's `order::Vehicle`, `in_flight_read` and `Carries`, and the emitter's statement grouping. ADR-033 stops being provisional by being **displaced** rather than by being measured, and its status line says so.

### Fixed (a task that never finishes no longer hangs the program)

> This one was introduced and fixed inside this release, and the two entries it
> had are one: the drain that makes a task nobody joins still run is what made a
> task that never finishes hold the program, and the bound is what it had been
> missing.

- Holding `main`'s value until the started queue empties is what makes ADR-055 D5's *"a task nobody joins still runs"* true, and it meant a task that never completes never let the program exit. **[ADR-006](docs/specification/adr/adr-006.md) D5 already covered this** — *"waits for parked cleanups **and detached tasks**, bounded by `cleanup-deadline`"* — so nothing here is a new rule, only the half of an old one that had never been built.
- The clock starts when `main`'s value arrives and not before, because what the deadline bounds is the wait for the tasks and `main` itself may run for as long as it likes. `"0"` disables draining, which is that decision's own word for it. On expiry the program says how many tasks it abandoned and what the bound was, rather than exiting quietly.
- **The park takes the remaining time with it** while draining, so a worker that never answers cannot become a program that never exits. The honest limit is D5's own: the timer is checked *between* parks rather than driven independently, because a single-threaded executor has no second thread to drive one from.

### Documented (what `overlap` met rather than made)

- **`let` takes one name, and the specification writes it taking several.** Part I 8.1.2's own example is `let (user, rights, prefs) = overlap { … }` and Part II 12.5 writes `let (tx, rx) = channel::bounded(100)` — a form the specification uses twice, for two different constructs, and defines nowhere. An `overlap` is reached by its tuple in the meantime, which works and reads worse than what the page promises. In [#224](https://github.com/Nikaia-Language/Nikaia/issues/224) with both sites as its evidence.

### Added (`let big = 3000000000` compiles)

- **It looks like a mistake and is not one**, which is the whole reason to change it ([ADR-060](docs/specification/adr/adr-060.md)). The line is refused today in the backend's words — *"literal out of range for `i32`"* — about a type the program never wrote. Nothing about it is wrong: the number is a number and the program has said nothing about its size.
- **What the field does:** Go and Swift give the default a size big enough; C, C# and Kotlin let the literal take the first type from a list that holds it; Java needs an `L` and Rust refuses. This language was in the smaller camp by inheritance rather than by choice.
- **Kotlin's rule as a fallback rather than as the rule** (D1, D2). Where a use constrains the literal, the use decides, unchanged — `let small = 42` followed by a call taking an `i64` compiles today and keeps compiling. Where nothing asks, the literal takes the first type that holds it: `i32`, else `i64`. Kotlin taken whole would have cost the first half, and Part I 2.4's second example is exactly that program.
- **And it needs none of the inference it seemed to** (D3), which is what made it worth doing now rather than later. The fear was a use-site walk over a binding's scope, which nothing else in this compiler needs. A value an `i32` cannot hold has no second answer a use could ask for — an integer literal is never an `f64`, `u8` is narrower, and there is no wider integer — so the rule is: fits an `i32`, change nothing; does not, emit an `i64`.
- **And it was the one rule D3 said it would be.** `emit::integer_literal` writes a literal an `i32` does not hold as an `i64` and every other one exactly as before, so `let big = 3000000000` compiles and prints while `let small = 42` handed to a parameter taking an `i64` keeps compiling — the literal that fits carries no type of its own, so the use still decides. No use-site walk, no second inference, nothing else touched.
- **The value, and not the digits.** The negation is folded at the emitter's `Unary` arm rather than inside that rule: `-2147483648` arrives as a negation of `2147483648`, one past `i32::MAX`, and a rule reading the literal alone would widen the one number where widening is wrong. One further out, `-2147483649`, is an `i64` and keeps its sign. Three tests in `tests/literals.rs`.
- **What it does not reach is now a question rather than a gap.** `3000000000 + 1` compiles, because the first operand widened; `2000000000 + 2000000000` is still refused, because neither operand is out of range and the sum is not a literal. That the two lines differ is not predictable from Part I 2.4, so it was a question with what either direction costs, since answered by [ADR-063](docs/specification/adr/adr-063.md) — D3's "no analysis" is exactly what folding a sum in the emitter would spend. Part I 2.2's note says which of the two is which.
- Part I 2.4's status note says built, both halves. the former backlog file is **empty** and §2 is one entry shorter.

### Changed (`access` reads, `update` writes, and no lambda is handed something mutable)

- **A question that stopped being one** ([ADR-059](docs/specification/adr/adr-059.md)). `access`'s block mutated through its parameter, and a lambda's parameter has no spelling that says it may be — so the choice looked like "add a spelling" against "let mutability arrive invisibly from the callee's contract". Two facts, looked up: the rule that a reader sees `mut` is unbroken across every program in this repository, and the grammar's one place where a callee may change what it was handed is spelled — `&mut self`.
- **And the door's justification was a cost that is not there.** `access` exists because *"a list of ten thousand entries is not copied to append one"*. `let mut v = old` inside `update` lowers to `let mut v = old;` — a **move**, three words, whatever the size. `update` could already append without copying, with the mutation spelled by the word this language has, in the place it has it.
- So `access` **reads** in place and may not change what it is handed (D1) — the one thing neither other door does, since `get()` copies and `update` must return the new state. `update` is **where locked data changes** (D2), and `old` is an ordinary immutable parameter. Therefore no lambda is handed something it may change, and there is nothing to spell (D3) — Part I 5.3's one lambda form untouched, and the reversible direction taken: a spelling can still be added later, where shipping invisible mutability and requiring a word for it afterwards would have invalidated every lambda already written.
- All four doors are built on both shapes of [ADR-057](docs/specification/adr/adr-057.md), the value sits in an `Option` so `update` moves it out and back without a `Default` bound or unsafe code, and a lambda that fails leaves the lock **empty** — reported as that rather than read as something else. `std.contracts` describes all four.
- **`access` moves sides in the ordering rule**: it is a read now, so two `access`es of one lock are unordered like two `get`s, and the writing forms are `set` and `update`.
- **What it costs, found while building and not after:** `access_all` reads and `update` writes **one**, so Chapter 12's own transfer between two accounts — take from one, give to the other, under both locks — has no door. Part II 12.2 carries a status note saying so and [#245](https://github.com/Nikaia-Language/Nikaia/issues/245) carries the entry; what such a door is called is a decision and not a footnote.
- One behaviour, kept: a shared borrow would have let a nested `access` through on the cheap shape while the crossing shape's owner check refused it, which is two behaviours for one written type. Reading is exclusive too, so re-entering a lock is a defect through whichever door it happens.

### Changed (`open-decisions.md` lists what is open, and nothing else)

- **The file carried nine entries of which none was open** — eight answered and one dropped, each kept with its full reasoning beside a heading saying which ADR had answered it. That is two copies of every answer, and the copy on a notes page is the one that goes stale: three of its headings had already drifted this session alone. It now holds **six entries and every one of them is open** — the five that were genuinely unanswered, plus the `std::http` question a parallel session put while this was being rewritten — and the answers are where they belong.
- **Nothing was lost on the way out.** Each departing entry was diffed against its record first. One real gap turned up: [ADR-053](docs/specification/adr/adr-053.md) mentioned *"the alternative answers"* in passing without saying what they were or why each failed — that a package-identity module name pulls the registry question forward and widens a check written for `use` lines, and that nesting the modules contradicts [ADR-047](docs/specification/adr/adr-047.md) D2 rule 3. Both are in that record now, with what each costs. Everything else was already in ADR-046 through ADR-055.
- **The citations point at the records now**, which is the same rule one level down: eleven sites in the compiler, the tests, the specification records and `docs/error-corpus.md` cited `open-decisions.md §5`, `§7` or `§9` for answers that ADR-050, ADR-051 and ADR-055 hold. A notes-page section number is the worst possible anchor for a decision — it renumbers whenever an entry closes, which is what this change does to all nine.
- **What is open, with what blocks each:** what `access` hands its lambda (the surface of `Locked[T]`, which [ADR-057](docs/specification/adr/adr-057.md) left undecided and Part II 12.2's own example needs); whether an un-annotated integer literal has a type (the last `NK1116`-class defect, which cannot be widened without refusing a correct program); whether the language has an unconditional loop (nothing is half-built, which is why it is a decision and not work); what a program may do at compile time ([ADR-026](docs/specification/adr/adr-026.md) is Open and holds the six questions — the entry names Q4 as the one blocking the others rather than restating them); and how a package is named by a version.
- **The line for what belongs is drawn, and it is broader than "blocks work".** `std::http` blocks no work at all and belongs anyway: it blocks *reading* an accepted record whose surface half cannot be evaluated, which is a cost that grows silently. What does not belong is a question nothing rests on — which SQLite binding `std::db` would use is undecided and blocks nothing, because `std::db` does not exist in any form. That is scope, the roadmap holds it, and scope becomes a decision when something comes to rest on it.
- Fixed on the way past: [ADR-033](docs/specification/adr/adr-033.md) §8 still said a non-literal argument *"needs a decision about what may cross a thread"*. [ADR-045](docs/specification/adr/adr-045.md) took that decision — per value **and** destination — so what remains there is the widening and not a ruling.

### Changed (the specification's status notes catch up with the execution model)

- **Part I 8.1 *"Async by Default"* had no status note at all**, and it was the sentence that most needed one: *"functions that perform I/O automatically pause execution without blocking the whole program"* was not true, because the emitted Rust contained the word `async` zero times and at `user_parallelism = no` the blocked thread **is** the program. Every sentence in that section was a promise about a lowering nobody had written. It now says what is built, what still is not, and that *"you do not write a keyword"* is checked by a test that reads the corpus rather than promised.
- **Part II 11.1 *"Implicit Async & The Scheduler"* likewise had none.** Its `no` column is built; its `yes` column — a work-stealing scheduler — is not, and the note says why `rayon` is not it.
- **Part II 11.2's `@detached` note said `spawn` does not lower and the capture it decides is not reported.** Both are built. The replacement also states the *narrowness* of the move rule, which is the part worth knowing: only a type that is known and that a move takes away, so a number, a `char` and a view are not it, a `Shared[T]` handle is exempt, and an assignment in between clears it.
- **Part I 8.4's *"the sidecar exists; the yield point does not"*** — the yield point exists now, for files. A database call and standard input are not that yet, and the note says which is which rather than leaving the bullet reading as done.
- **Part II 12.1 gained a note because `sync` changed job.** It was a claim the compiler checked and nothing acted on; it now decides whether a function is compiled as `async fn` or plain `fn`, which makes ADR-027's conservatism load-bearing and a regression in the inference a regression in the output. Measured: 22 `sync` against 17 that can pause, across `examples/`.
- **Part II 12.7's `task::scope` note** says what it would now be built *on*, since the executor that owns tasks and the `spawn` that feeds it both exist — so what a scope adds is the waiting and the touch propagation, not a mechanism.
- Part I 8.1.2's `overlap` note and Part III 13.3's `user_parallelism` note no longer say `spawn` is unbuilt.

### Changed (the roadmap and the open-decisions page catch up with the execution model)

- **The roadmap's phases carried no item for the async lowering at all.** Phase 0 is *"The Execution Model"* and named only [ADR-033](docs/specification/adr/adr-033.md); a reader would not have learnt from it that a Nikaia program is now `async`, has an executor, suspends at a file read, or can `spawn`. Phase 0 now has both records, with what each has built, what building it corrected, what the record claimed and building it disproved, and what is open — and the ✅ status list has the line it was missing.
- **The "what is next" paragraph said this was the head of the list**, which it is not any more: four of the five steps are built at the default setting, so what is left of it needs a *thread* or is `overlap`, and the rest of the former backlog file's order can be taken as it stands.
- **`open-decisions.md` was missing the decision this session actually asked for.** The question *"what does a task mean at `user_parallelism = no`?"* is exactly what that page is for — it blocked the largest item in [#219](https://github.com/Nikaia-Language/Nikaia/issues/219), it could not be answered from the code, and the answer changed what the compiler emits. It is §9 now, with why it had to be asked, the three readings a synchronous lowering allowed and what each broke, and what the answer cost. §5's heading said `overlap` waits on the runtime binding `spawn` waits on; the binding is built, so it says what `overlap` can lean on instead.
- **Four status notes that had gone stale**: Part I 5.4's *"the capture it decides is not reported yet"* (`NK2101` is raised now), Part I 8.1.1's `overlap` note and Part III 13.3's `user_parallelism` note (both said `spawn` is not built), and `docs/spec-promises.md`'s diagnostic lists — those last are left as they were, with a note saying so, because that page's whole value is being readable against the day it was written.
- `task::both` is named as *the pool's vehicle* where the roadmap and [ADR-033](docs/specification/adr/adr-033.md) describe it, because it is one of two now: D10's question is unchanged and the answer has a second arm.
### Added (`Locked[T]` has a shape, and it is decided per value)

- **Neither per build setting nor a lower bound under both** ([ADR-057](docs/specification/adr/adr-057.md)). Part II 12.2 decided it per setting — a borrow flag at `user_parallelism = no`, an OS mutex at `yes` — which puts a value's ability to cross a thread in the hands of whoever *builds the program*. The investigated alternative, a mutex everywhere, charges 11.3 ns an acquisition at `no`, which is exactly what that switch exists to save. The third answer was already in the building: the reference count asks this question per value and answers it.
- **The safe shape is the floor** (D1), the polarity the count analysis already runs on. **At one user thread every lock is the cheap shape** (D2): nothing a user writes can cross there, and the cheap shape keeps the only diagnostic reachable at that setting — a bare mutex hangs for ever instead, taking [ADR-006](docs/specification/adr/adr-006.md) D5's shutdown deadline with it. **At several it follows the value** (D3), off the same analysis and with all seven of its reasons to decline unchanged.
- **The two shapes report the same thing when a program re-enters one lock** (D4), which is what makes choosing between them invisible to a reader — `Rc` and `Arc` differ in cost and nothing else, a borrow flag and a bare mutex differ in behaviour. The mutex shape carries an owner check for it, measured at +2.0 ns, ×1.15 (`docs/mutex-floor.md` §4.3).
- The annotation allocates **both** hulls, because there is no `Locked::new` in the language any more than there is a `Shared::new`; `Locked::access` is in `std.contracts` with `sync = "from(f)"`, which is the entry `docs/mutex-floor.md` §3.1 found missing and what makes Part II 12.2's own idiom `sync`; and both shapes translate back to `Locked` in a relayed message like every other substituted name.
- **Not built, and named in the record rather than left to be found:** what `access` hands its lambda (Part II 12.2's `counter.access fn(n) { n + 1 }` does not compile as written — a question about the surface), and the analysis watching a `Shared[Locked[T]]` allocation, without which the cheap shape never triggers at `yes`.
- `crates/nikaia/tests/lock_floor.rs` stays a **probe of both answers**: it now cuts the shipped `Locked::access` entry out before putting a variant in, so the decision keeps its evidence instead of only its conclusion.
